title: Agreement between subject and verb 2
subtitle: a number of people are / the number of people is
summary: Choose a singular or a plural verb after quantity phrases such as any of, none of, a number of and one of, and after subjects joined by and or or.

lesson.heading: any of, each of, either of, neither of, none of
lesson.text: With **any of, each of, either of, neither of** or **none of** and a plural noun or pronoun we can use either a singular or a plural verb. The singular verb is the safer choice in careful written English.

examples.text: I don't think any of them **knows** (or **know**) where the money is hidden.
Neither of the French athletes **has** (or **have**) won this year.

lesson.heading: a number of and the number of

left.label: a number of + plural noun
left.text: Plural verb. The same goes for a / the majority of, a lot of, plenty of, all (of) and some (of) with a plural noun.
examples: A number of refugees **have** been turned back at the border.
The majority of those questioned **think** that the policies have failed.

right.label: the number of + plural noun
right.text: Singular verb - the subject is one figure, not many things.
examples: The number of books in the library **has** risen to over five million.

lesson.heading: one of ...
lesson.text: After **one of** and a plural noun or pronoun we use a singular verb. However, after **one of + plural noun + who** either verb is often possible, and the plural one is more grammatical.

examples.text: **One of the reasons** I took the job **was** that I could work from home.
He's one of those teachers who **insist** / **insists** on pupils sitting silently in class.

lesson.heading: Uncountable nouns, every, each, everyone
lesson.text: With **any of, none of, the majority of, a lot of, plenty of, all (of)** or **some (of)** and an uncountable noun we use a singular verb. **Every** and **each** with a singular noun (or a coordinated noun *x and y*) also take a singular verb, and so do **everyone, everybody, everything** and the similar words in *any-, some-* and *no-*.

examples.text: All the furniture **was** destroyed in the fire.
None of the equipment **appears** to be damaged.
Every boy and girl **takes** part in the activity.

examples.note: but The children have each drawn a picture.

examples.text: Practically everyone **thinks** that Phil should be given the job.

lesson.heading: Items joined by and
lesson.text: When a subject has two or more items joined by **and**, we usually use a plural verb. But phrases connected by *and* can take a singular verb if we think of them as making up a single item.

examples.text: Ingrid and Tobias **are** moving back to Australia.
The lorry, its cargo and passengers **weighs** around 35 tonnes.
examples.note: or ... weigh ... - the three together make up one load

lesson.heading: (either) ... or ..., (neither) ... nor ...
lesson.text: Here the verb agrees with the **last** item: a singular verb if the last item is singular, a plural verb if it is plural. If the last item is singular and the one before it is plural, both verbs are possible.

examples.text: Either the station or the cinema **is** a good place to meet.
The President or his representatives **are** to attend the meeting.
Either the teachers or the principal **is** to blame for the accident.

lesson.heading: there + be / have
lesson.text: After **there** we use a singular verb form with singular and uncountable nouns and a plural form with plural nouns. In informal speech, though, a shortened singular form (*There's*) is often used with plural nouns.

examples.text: Over the last few years there **have been** many improvements in car safety.
**There's been** lots of good films on lately.
examples.note: or There've been ... - informal speech only

lesson.text: In careful writing prefer the singular verb after *none of, neither of* and *any of* - and never forget that *the number of* always takes a singular verb.

exercises.prompt: A number of refugees ___ been turned back at the border.
exercises.explanation: a number of + plural noun takes a plural verb.

exercises.prompt: The number of books in the library ___ risen to over five million.
exercises.explanation: the number of is the exception: it refers to one figure, so the verb is singular.

exercises.prompt: I'd be surprised if any of my children ___ my birthday.
exercises.explanation: After any of + plural noun both forms are possible; remembers is preferred in careful written English.

exercises.statement: Plenty of jobs is available, but no one wants them because they're so poorly paid.
exercises.explanation: Plenty of jobs are available, but no one wants them because they're so poorly paid. plenty of + plural noun takes a plural verb.

exercises.prompt: In careful written English, does each subject take a singular or a plural verb?
I don't think any of ___ particularly good. In fact, the restaurant is rather disappointing.
exercises.explanation: food is uncountable, so after any of the verb has to be singular.

exercises.statement: A number of medicines relieve the symptoms of influenza, but none can cure it.
exercises.explanation: Correct. a number of + plural noun takes a plural verb (relieve).

exercises.prompt: Mainly because of recent health scares involving beef and chicken, the number of vegetarians ___ to rise dramatically in the next five years.
exercises.explanation: the number of takes a singular verb, so the passive is is expected.

exercises.prompt: Why did you take the job? Put the words in order.
exercises.answer: One of the reasons I took the job was that I could work from home.
exercises.explanation: After one of + plural noun the verb is singular: was.

exercises.prompt: The majority of those questioned ___ that the government's economic policies have failed.
exercises.explanation: the majority of + plural noun takes a plural verb.

exercises.prompt: Over the last few years there ___ many improvements in car safety.
exercises.explanation: there + a plural noun takes a plural verb form: there have been.

exercises.prompt: Professor Smith and Dr Peters claim that the wreck of the ship and its cargo ___ a danger to local people fishing near the island.
exercises.explanation: The wreck and its cargo act together as a single item, so the singular constitutes is more likely.
